I'll offer a personal opinion, and I'm sure others here might have a different take on it.

MJ can be very helpful for depression, but it is not a good long-term solution. I think it is of the most value when combined with therapy from a sensible, trusted shrink.

Depression makes everything hard, and that includes getting over depression. It's like a computer virus that comes in and the first thing it does is it kills your antivirus program. Depression lies. It makes you believe your therapy is worthless, and they there is no hope, no reason to follow through. That's how it wins.

When you smoke some weed the depression and hopelessness lift for a while. The lie goes away. You can remember what it's like to feel good, and you can see which direction to go. But then you sober up and you're right back where you were. Smoke it every day and it just becomes the new normal, and you become a depressed person who's too stoned to really care. That's not what you want.

Find a shrink who you respect - somebody who is smart enough that you'd be willing to listen to their advice, and who jives with you enough that you can spill your guts. Don't try to be likable, just vomit up everything bad, all your insecurities and all the things you hate most about yourself. If you can do that, and smoke weed occasionally during the process, I think you've got a really good combination happening.

Well here's some basic beginner advice then...

It's kind of like booze in that you don't want to do too much, or you can feel kinda miserable. That's pretty much the only way to do it wrong. Unlike booze, it really won't hurt you after the discomfort passes, and it can be helpful to keep that in mind. If you do get uncomfortable, just lie down and it will go away on it's own.

It's also not uncommon for beginners to not get high the first or second time they try it. You can see how this can lead to making mistake number one.

Be in a comfortable place with nothing you have to do for a few hours, no responsibilities. Take one hit from your vape or pipe, maybe two, no more than that. Then wait about five minutes. If everything is not really awesome, take another hit. If nothing is happening, try again a couple of days later.

The dispensary should be able to help you out with picking a strain and a vape so I'll let them teach you that part. Stay away from dabs or wax, they are very, very strong. I'd also suggest avoiding edibles until you are a comfortably experienced user, because dosage can be very unpredictable.

I like to smoke between maybe 4pm and 6pm, any later than that and it can make it harder to get to sleep.

It's a new feeling. Embrace it and just kind of let it do its thing.

Just a note, cannabis can sometimes increase anxiety. I think this can mostly be solved by being in a relaxed setting, preferably with some people you trust and won't judge you. If you are not fortunate enough to have people like that in your life (at one point I wasn't) then just do it at home where you are most comfortable. However, cannabis increases your heart rate and decreases blood pressure, which can sometimes feel like a panic attack.

Remember, relax...it is supposed to feel different. If you start to feel like you aren't liking it, take some deep breaths and turn on the TV or some music to distract you and remember that the feeling will subside after a little bit.

I started experimenting around the beginning of the year, primarily to see how it helped me get along. I think I may have more of anxiety as a root cause that leads to depression, but here's what I've found from the experience so far. (For context, I got a quarter ounce and an Arizer Air. Works great, I enjoy the clean high, and that quarter lasted me from February to almost the beginning of June.) It helped me in two ways: if I really needed to just let go, I could get pretty ripped and do that successfully, but in low doses it actually helps me be much more productive. I think that's because it slowed things down enough that I lose the ability to have a bunch of different competing thoughts going on at once. It calms down to one thread, which helps me be more decisive and objective. Working that into a normal routine means that all of the time I would spend spiraling started to be spent getting things done. Nothing fancy, I didn't suddenly start going "time to make all of my dreams come true!"

It was better than that. Instead, I could focus on getting my work done and doing it well. Chores are immensely more enjoyable while high, which means I don't mind spending the time to do dishes and laundry and clean up my apartment. It also hugely curbed my drinking, I didn't need to get buzzed to fall asleep -- I could actually just enjoy a nice beer with dinner and be perfectly content.

I think the benefit of incorporating chiba into daily life isn't necessarily that it suddenly makes your depression/anxiety go away. (Also, as other people noted it's possible that it can exacerbate anxiety in some people, I have a few armchair theories about it but it's still something to be aware of.) Rather, in my experience, it took some of the pressure off and helped me engage in other healthy behaviors. And each of those behaviors would then make it easier to weather the storm if I had a bad week and things were getting me down, because then I had this whole routine of activities that were helpful and productive and genuinely improved my life. As of now I've been dankrupt for a few weeks, and I'm noticing that it's getting increasingly difficult to keep it all up, because now I'm lacking what was helping me get and keep that healthy momentum going. It obviously differs from person to person, but for me I do see it as a long term solution to help me live a good life that my biology tends to get in the way of.

Best of luck! Envious of the states where it's legally available, hopefully it won't be too long before it breaks through to where I'm at.
